Absolute ideology and candidate performance

Ideology and Electoral Performance

This page tests whether ideological position helps explain why some Alabama legislative candidates ran ahead of their districts. The comparison uses absolute national ideology, individual issue positions, and performance against CMO, same-cycle federal results, and the previous presidential vote.

Summary: More conservative Democratic officeholders performed better against multiple electoral baselines. The issue evidence points to a culturally conservative but economically mixed coalition. Coverage is strongest among winners and incumbents, so these results describe historical candidates more confidently than unknown challengers.

The quantity being explained

The outcome is measured before ideology is added

Context CMO is calculated without candidate ideology, incumbency, finance, or prior candidate performance. Ideology is introduced afterward as a possible explanation for the residual rather than as part of the expectation being explained.

Actual candidate marginLegislative two-party result

Ideology-blind expectationDistrict, cycle, chamber, and baseline context

Positive candidate-directional values always mean that the named candidate—Democrat or Republican—ran ahead. One voter switching parties changes a two-party margin twice as much as one additional base voter, but aggregate election results cannot distinguish persuasion from turnout.

Absolute position

Absolute ideology and federal-relative performance

Each point is one candidate-cycle with a nationally comparable Shor–McCarty score. Use the controls to change the electoral baseline or isolate a party; the axes and summary update with the selection.

Democratic candidateRepublican candidate
Absolute ideology: more liberal ← national scale → more conservativeCandidate overperformance vs federal baseline →National midpoint
Democrats

Moving one national standard deviation rightward is associated with greater federal-relative performance. The relationship survives winner-only, prior-service, finance, incumbency, and leave-one-cycle-out checks.

Republicans

Point estimates generally favor less conservative Republicans, but most are imprecise. A winner-only CMO result is suggestive; federal-relative and prior-service results do not establish a general moderation advantage.

Support and selection

Coverage is concentrated among successful candidates

The Democratic and Republican distributions have little common support, and Shor–McCarty primarily observes people who reached office. The selection audit shows how different the scored sample is from candidates without an observed score.

Mechanism decomposition

Total association and mediator-adjusted association

The first estimate leaves incumbency and fundraising out because electoral strength may help produce both. The second conditions on them. The difference between the bars shows how much of the relationship is absorbed by those possible pathways.

For Democrats, the absolute relationship remains strong for CMO and federal-relative performance after adding incumbency and finance. Presidential-relative performance attenuates in the smaller finance-complete sample.

Individual issues

Issue-level associations are not one left–right scale

The issue chart keeps substantively different positions separate. It does not combine gun access with criminal punishment, racial civil rights with sexual morality, or the level of taxation with who bears the tax.

These are separate historical associations, not additive points in a single score. False-discovery-adjusted values are shown. Tax burden does not say who paid the tax and must not be read as generic fiscal conservatism.

District fit

District fit varies by issue

A positive interaction means conservative positioning becomes more favorable as a district's federal vote becomes more Republican. Several issue interactions appear, but uneven coverage and multiple testing make them leads for case research rather than forecast inputs.

Time and robustness

The aggregate relationship is durable; recent coverage is thin

The Democratic Shor coefficient remains positive when every cycle is omitted in turn. But only five post-2016 Democratic candidate-cycles have usable Shor scores, so the page does not manufacture a modern-era conclusion from an underpowered cell.

Method and limits

Interpretation and limits

1. Freeze the outcomeIdeology never enters expected CMO.
2. Use absolute positionNational Shor scores replace within-caucus rank.
3. Orient by partyRightward Democrats and leftward Republicans are tested separately.
4. Separate mechanismsTotal and mediator-adjusted estimates answer different questions.
5. Prefer federal baselinesSame-cycle federal and prior-presidential performance test durability.
6. Split issue axesGuns, race, sexuality, taxation, and public order remain distinct.
7. Audit selectionWinner and prior-service sensitivities constrain interpretation.
8. Do not forecast yetCandidate ideology lacks prospective challenger coverage.

This is historical, observational evidence. Shor scores are career measures and cover successful officeholders disproportionately. Issue evidence is temporally screened but uneven. Associations can reflect recruitment, geography, candidate quality, and coalition composition as well as voter response.
